title: Germanicus Allegedly Poisoned by Magic; Trial Follows
description: When Germanicus Julius Caesar fell ill and died in 19 CE (initially reported with earlier symptoms in 17 CE), accusations immediately arose that he had been killed by magical means at the instigation of Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso and his wife Plancina. Tacitus reports that remains of human bodies, blood-soaked ashes, leaden tablets with curses, and other magical apparatus were found buried beneath the floor of his residence. This case illustrates how magical causation was invoked to explain elite deaths and how such accusations became tools in political rivalry. Piso was subsequently tried and died before the verdict, likely by suicide.
historiographical_note: The Germanicus case has been analyzed by Matthew Dickie and Richard Gordon as a key example of how defixiones (curse tablets) and magical apparatus were used as evidence in Roman trials, directly paralleling later witchcraft prosecution evidence.
